questions.stem: In the beginning phase of treatment, what would a Narrative Therapy therapist do?

options.C: Identify treatment focus and goals.

questions.stem: In the beginning phase of treatment, what would a Object Relations therapist do?

options.B: Attunement is the key intervention in the early stage and consists of forging a personal relationship between the therapist and the patient.
options.C: Provide “experience-near” empathy
options.D: Collaboratively identifying client’s “attachment style," that is, problematic behavioral and emotional patterns, formed in early childhood as attempts to maintain attachment to primary caregivers.

questions.stem: In the beginning phase of treatment, what would a Object Relations therapist do?

options.B: Collaboratively identifying client’s “attachment style," that is, problematic behavioral and emotional patterns, formed in early childhood as attempts to maintain attachment to primary caregivers.
options.C: Build rapport and therapeutic alliance through listening
options.D: Explore the client's problem and history, including relationship history.

questions.stem: In the middle phase of treatment, what would a Object Relations therapist do?

options.A: Addressing enactments: situations in the therapy may have played out in the past, or outside in the client’s life. Being able to talk about in session together. “It sounds like what’s going on with your partner is similar to what happened with your father.”
options.B: Empathizing with losses and blows to self.
options.C: Promote insight and growth through interpretation.
options.D: Identify alternative self-objects: people they did have had positive relationship with them. Through their relationship with T they learn about different positive selfobjects, and can start to identify healthy selfobjects for themselves.

questions.stem: In the middle phase of treatment, what would a Object Relations therapist do?

options.A: Repair disruptions of the self-object transference
options.B: Identify alternative self-objects: people they did have had positive relationship with them. Through their relationship with T they learn about different positive selfobjects, and can start to identify healthy selfobjects for themselves.
options.C: Mourning loss of selfobjects Mourning the mother they may have never had. They can grieve these losses. An acceptance of that loss, a sadness that is allowed to happen over it. Cry for their younger selves, inner child.
options.D: Confront (aka bringing the issues to attention: I notice when I bring this up, you quickly change the subject) resistance and primitive defense mechanisms.

questions.stem: In the end phase of treatment, what would a Object Relations therapist do?

options.A: Repair occurs during the late middle phase and the end of treatment.
options.B: Acknowledge and process issues related to termination.
options.C: Reflect on the treatment process
options.D: Work through termination and abandonment issues.

questions.stem: In the middle phase of treatment, what would a Self Psychology therapist do?

options.A: Disruptions are explored in the middle phase. Disruptions include those in the early life of the client as well as those in current relationships, including the relationship with the therapist. Where they are having conflicts, where there is pain, disruptions in attunement. Can even apply to what happens in the therapy room, between client and the therapist.
options.B: Addressing enactments: situations in the therapy may have played out in the past, or outside in the client’s life. Being able to talk about in session together. “It sounds like what’s going on with your partner is similar to what happened with your father.”
options.C: Support client’s ability to regulate and express emotions in relationally difficult Situations teaching clients to have a reflective stance toward themselves.

questions.stem: In the end phase of treatment, what would a Self Psychology therapist do?

options.C: Repair stage of the therapy aims to alter the patient’s current reactions to the events that cause them emotional distress by sharing their own interpretations of the event. By sharing their own subjective interpretation, the therapist helps create a new reality of the painful events for the patient in order to get rid of unwanted emotions and reactions.
options.D: Consolidate interpretations.

questions.stem: In the beginning phase of treatment, what would a Experiential / Symbolic Therapy (Whitaker) therapist do?

options.B: Beginning: Engage family as authentic people. Battle for structure. Encourage all members to attend. Family wins battle of initiative. Gather information about boundaries, coalitions, roles, and level of conflict.
options.C: both accommodate to and challenge rules of family system
options.D: assessment/mapping of hierarchy alignments, and boundaries

questions.stem: In the middle phase of treatment, what would a Experiential / Symbolic Therapy (Whitaker) therapist do?

options.A: Support and strengthen each individual’s sense of uniqueness and self-esteem.
options.C: utilize enactments of issues to challenge participants and unbalance the system.
options.D: Middle: Develop sense of cohesion. Create alternative interactions. Highlight inappropriate boundaries (highlighting when family member pushes their world view on others for example). Role-play situations. Use play and “craziness.”

questions.stem: In the end phase of treatment, what would a Experiential / Symbolic Therapy (Whitaker) therapist do?

options.B: Help family practice implement and integrate changes and increase awareness of larger familial patterns.
options.C: End: Highlight accomplishments and reflect on growth. Identify possible blocks to future growth. Role-play future scenarios. Each member expresses feelings about their experience of therapy.
options.D: reinforce structural change
